A_target.statement:
Let $\sequence {x_n}$ be a [[Definition:Bounded Real Sequence|bounded real sequence]].
Then $\sequence {x_n}$ has a [[Definition:Convergent Real Sequence|convergent]] [[Definition:Subsequence|subsequence]].

B_source.statement:
Let $I_0 = \closedint a b$.
Repeatedly [[Definition:Bisection|bisect]] the current interval, keeping a half $I_{k + 1} \subseteq I_k$ which retains a given property.
Then the lengths satisfy $\size {I_k} = 2^{-k} \paren {b - a}$.

substitutions.the property retained at each halving: containing infinitely many terms of the sequence
substitutions.the nested intervals produced: intervals whose lengths halve at each step
substitutions.the point common to all intervals: the limit of the extracted subsequence

derived.the nested interval intersection: a single point, since the lengths tend to zero
derived.the terms chosen inside each interval: a subsequence converging to that point

validity_conditions: At least one half of any interval containing infinitely many terms again contains infinitely many, which is what makes the invariant maintainable.
The interval lengths halve each time and so tend to zero, so the nested intersection is a single point by completeness of the reals.
Choosing one term from each interval with strictly increasing index is possible precisely because each interval contains infinitely many terms.
proof_plan:
As $\sequence {x_n}$ is [[Definition:Bounded Real Sequence|bounded]], there exists $I_0 = \closedint a b$ containing every $x_n$.
Thus $I_0$ contains $x_n$ for infinitely many $n$.

Halve $I_k$.
At least one half contains $x_n$ for infinitely many $n$; let $I_{k + 1}$ be such a half.
From the [[Nested Intervals Theorem]], $\displaystyle \bigcap_k I_k = \set l$ for a unique $l$, since $\size {I_k} \to 0$.

Choose $n_1 < n_2 < \cdots$ with $x_{n_k} \in I_k$.
Then $\size {x_{n_k} - l} \le 2^{-k} \paren {b - a} \to 0$.
Hence $x_{n_k} \to l$.
{{qed}}
